title: The Holes in Geometry's First Proof

source.title: Proposition 1
source.authors: Euclid (the modern Guide and critiques are not attributed in the text)

intro.summary: Proposition 1, the first result of Euclid's Elements, asks how to build an equilateral triangle (all three sides equal) on a given line segment AB. Euclid draws two circles, one centred at A and one centred at B, each with radius AB. He joins the point C where they cross to A and B. He then argues that all three sides equal AB, so they equal each other. The modern commentary shows that this short, clear proof has logical gaps. Nothing in Euclid's starting rules guarantees that the circles cross at all. Nothing shows that the figure lies flat in a plane. Nothing rules out the two sides merging before they reach C, which was the objection of Zeno of Sidon. The source is one short proposition with commentary, not a survey: it names the missing assumptions but does not supply a complete repaired axiom system. It also notes a historical disagreement. Posidonius claimed to refute Zeno, and the commentator judges that refutation faulty. Good follow-up topics are how later mathematicians, such as Hilbert, filled these gaps with continuity and order axioms, Euclid's treatment of meeting circles in Book III, and Proposition I.22, which needs the same circle-intersection assumption.
background: A circle is all the points at the same distance from one centre point, and that distance is called the radius.
An equilateral triangle is a three-sided flat shape whose three sides all have the same length, like a standard road warning sign.
Euclid built geometry from a short list of starting rules (postulates, definitions and 'common notions') and tried to justify every later step from them.
Euclid's constructions use only two tools: a straightedge for drawing straight lines and a compass for drawing circles.
intro.aha: Euclid's very first proof, the one that looks too obvious to question, quietly relies on facts his own rules never state: that the two circles actually cross, and that two straight lines cannot run together and share a stretch.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Suppose you are handed a straight line segment AB, like a stick lying on a table. Can you build a triangle on it with all three sides exactly as long as the stick, using only a ruler without markings and a compass? This is the first problem in Euclid's Elements, a geometry book written over 2,000 years ago.
primer.quote: To construct an equilateral triangle on a given finite straight line.

primer.heading: What Euclid did
primer.body: Euclid draws a circle centred at A that passes through B. He draws a second circle centred at B that passes through A. Where the two circles cross, he marks a point C and joins it to A and to B. Every point on a circle is the same distance from its centre, so AC equals AB and BC equals AB. Things equal to the same thing are equal to each other, so all three sides match.
primer.quote: And things which equal the same thing also equal one another, therefore AC also equals BC.

primer.heading: What the critics found
primer.body: The proof looks complete, but critics over many centuries have found steps that Euclid's rules never justify. The biggest gap is the point C. Euclid simply assumes the two circles cross, and none of his postulates says they must. Two further gaps concern the triangle itself. Nothing shows that the three sides lie flat in a plane. Nothing shows that sides AC and BC don't merge into one line before they reach C.
primer.quote: It is surprising that such a short, clear, and understandable proof can be so full of holes.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and what is uncertain
primer.body: A drawing can convince your eyes without proving anything. The commentary notes that some versions of geometry exist where these circles never meet, so an extra assumption is truly needed. The critics did not all agree. Posidonius claimed to have answered Zeno of Sidon's objection, and the commentator judges that answer faulty. The source names what is missing, such as 'two straight lines meet in at most one point', but leaves the full repair to later work.
primer.quote: There are models of geometry in which the circles do not intersect.
primer.quote_where: Guide, Why does the point C exist?

concepts.title: Every point on a circle is equally far from the centre
concepts.idea: A circle is defined as all the points at one fixed distance from its centre, so any point you pick on it is exactly one radius away.

predict.question: A circle has centre A and passes through a point B. A new point C sits on the same circle, on the far side from B. Without measuring, how does the length AC compare with AB?
options: AC is exactly equal to AB
AC is longer, because C is farther round the circle from B
AC is shorter, because C is on the other side
You can't tell without a ruler
why: Right: B and C are both on a circle centred at A, so each is exactly one radius from A. That makes AC equal to AB, wherever C sits.
Going farther round the edge feels like going farther away. But the distance that matters is the straight line from the centre, and that stays the radius all the way round.
Being on the opposite side changes the direction from A, not the length. Every point on the edge is the same straight-line distance from A.
A ruler would only confirm it. The definition of a circle already guarantees that every point on it is one radius from the centre. This is how the proof gets AC = AB without measuring anything.

terms.means: Equally far. Every point on a circle is equidistant from its centre.
Euclid's definition of a circle in Book I. The proof cites it in the margin when it uses the fact that every point on the circle is one radius from the centre.

model.title: A circle around A, with a point P you can slide along its edge
model.note: Teaching model: the circle sits on a grid with centre A at (0, 0), and the distance from A to P is worked out with a coordinate formula. Euclid never used coordinates. He takes 'equal distance from the centre' straight from his definition of a circle. The positions and lengths are illustrative and are not from the paper.

controls.label: Where P sits around the circle

steps.say: Here is a circle. Its centre is the point A, right in the middle.
P is a point sitting on the edge of the circle. The line shows the straight path from A to P.
This slider slides P round the edge. Watch it travel.
This slider makes the whole circle bigger or smaller.
B is a fixed point. It never moves, whatever you do to the circle.
These boxes measure the distances as you play.

explore.prompt: Use what you just saw: the edge of the circle is everything exactly one radius from A. Make the circle and the point P meet B.

goals.text: Make the circle pass right through point B
hints: When does a circle go through a point? Think about how far that point is from the centre.
Read the 'Distance from A to B' box, then work with the Radius slider.
The edge reaches B once the radius matches the number in the 'Distance from A to B' box exactly.

goals.text: Land P exactly on top of B
hints: P can only ever sit on the circle, so the circle has to reach B first.
With the circle passing through B, slide P round until the 'Distance from P to B' box shrinks to almost nothing.
B is up and to the right of A, a little past halfway from the rightmost point of the circle to its top.

feedback.correct: Yes. B and C both lie on the circle centred at A, so each one is exactly one radius from A, and AC = AB. The proof uses this very step: point C lies on the circle centred at A, so AC equals AB.
feedback.incorrect: It is tempting to think that a point farther round the edge, or on the other side, is a different distance away. But a circle is defined as the points at one fixed distance from its centre. Every point on it is therefore the same straight-line distance from A, so AC = AB.

steps.say: Start simple. The radius is 2 and P sits at the far right of the circle. The distance from A to P reads 2.
Slide P up to the top. Its left–right and up–down positions have swapped completely. The distance from A? Still 2.
Send P down to the lower left. Both positions are now negative, but the line from A is exactly as long as before.
Every point on the edge is the same distance from A. The word for this is equidistant: equally far.
Euclid builds this into the meaning of 'circle'. The proof points to this definition in its margin as I.Def.15.
Now grow the circle. The distance from A to P changes, but only because the radius changed. Where P sits never matters.
Make it bigger still, then swing P right round. The distance from A to P stays fixed at the radius. B now sits inside the circle, closer to A than the edge is.

understand.explanation: A circle is not just a round shape. It is every point that lies at one fixed distance, the radius, from a centre. So if you know a point is on the circle, you know its distance from the centre without measuring. Euclid states this as a definition, not something he proves, and his proof of Proposition 1 leans on it twice. C lies on the circle centred at A, so AC equals AB, and C also lies on the circle centred at B, so BC equals BA. The model checks distances with a coordinate formula, which only illustrates the idea: in the proof the equal lengths come from the definition alone.
understand.quote: Now, since the point A is the center of the circle CDB, therefore AC equals AB. Again, since the point B is the center of the circle CAE, therefore BC equals BA.
understand.quote_where: Proposition 1, the proof (the step marked I.Def.15 in the margin)

connect.caption: The paper has no equation for this; Euclid simply writes 'AC equals AB'. This is the model's rule. P's left–right position (x_P) and up–down position (y_P) change as P slides round, but together they always give the same distance from A: the radius r. In the proof, C plays the part of P and AB is the radius.

concepts.recap: Any point on a circle is exactly one radius from its centre, so the proof can say AC = AB just because C lies on the circle centred at A.

concepts.title: Two circles build the triangle
concepts.idea: Two circles of radius AB, one centred at A and one at B, cross at a point C, and joining C to A and B gives a triangle on AB.

predict.question: A friend repeats the recipe on a segment AB three times longer than yours, and picks the crossing point below AB. You picked the one above. Compared with your triangle, theirs is…
options: The same shape, only bigger and flipped to the other side of AB
Taller and thinner, because bigger circles push C further away
Lopsided, because AC and BC come out different lengths
Flat, because C lands on the line AB
why: Right. Every length in the recipe is the radius AB, so stretching AB scales the whole picture evenly. The lower crossing is the mirror image of the upper one.
C does move further from AB, but A and B move apart by the same factor. Height and base grow together, so the shape stays the same.
C is on A's circle and on B's circle, which are the same size. So AC and BC are both one radius long, on either side of AB.
The circles cross away from the line AB, one crossing above it and one below. C never sits on AB, so A, B and C always form a real triangle.

terms.means: A point where two lines or curves cross, so it lies on both of them at once
A corner of a triangle, where two of its sides meet

model.title: Two circles of the same size, one around A and one around B, crossing at C
model.note: Teaching model: A sits at (−r/2, 0) and B at (r/2, 0) on a grid. The radius slider therefore also sets the length of AB, and the second circle around B uses that same radius, as Euclid's recipe requires. Lengths come from a coordinate formula, but Euclid used no coordinates or numbers. The picture is flat and simply draws the crossing points. What guarantees they exist comes later in the lesson. Lengths are illustrative and are not from the paper.

steps.say: Same picture as before: a circle around A, and a point P you can slide along it. One change: B now sits right on that circle, so the radius is exactly the distance from A to B.
New: a second circle of the same size, drawn around B. Where the two circles cross is C. Joining C to A and to B closes up a triangle.
The circles cross twice. This switch picks the crossing below AB instead of the one above. The radius slider now stretches AB and both circles together.

explore.prompt: Use P as a probe. It always stays on A's circle. Hunt for the spots that are also on B's circle, then build your own triangles.

goals.text: Slide P to a spot that is exactly as far from B as AB is long, so that P sits on both circles at once.
hints: P is already one radius from A, wherever it goes. Where is it also one radius from B?
Watch the 'Distance from P to B' box and slide P until it matches 'Length of AB'. P then lands where the two circles cross.
There are two such spots. The upper one is somewhere between 45° and 75° around A's circle.

goals.text: Build a triangle below AB with AB longer than 4, then park P exactly on its third corner C.
hints: Two things to change first: which slider makes AB longer, and which switch sends C below AB?
Then slide P round A's circle until the 'Distance from P to C' box drops to zero.
The lower crossing mirrors the upper one. Think of a full turn minus the angle you found for the upper crossing.

feedback.correct: Yes. Every length in the recipe is the one radius AB, so a longer AB just scales the whole figure. The paper notes that either crossing point will do, and the lower one gives the mirror image of the upper triangle.
feedback.incorrect: It is tempting to think bigger circles or the other crossing point change the shape. But C is always one radius from A and one radius from B, and the radius is always AB. So the triangle keeps its shape. It only grows, or flips to the other side of AB.

steps.say: Start with AB of length 2. Euclid's first move: draw a circle with centre A that passes through B, so its radius is AB.
Second move: draw a circle with centre B and radius BA. It is the same length, measured from the other end, so the two circles are the same size.

Remember that a circle is every point one radius from its centre. A point on both circles is one radius from A and also one radius from B. The spot where they cross is called an intersection point, and Euclid names it C.
Third move: join C to A and C to B with straight lines. Read the boxes. AC is 2 because C is on A's circle. BC is 2 because C is on B's circle.
C becomes the triangle's third corner, its vertex opposite AB. A triangle now stands on the given line AB.
Stretch AB to 4. Both circles grow together, C rises, and AB, AC and BC still all read the same length.
The circles cross twice, once above AB and once below. Flip the switch: the lower C gives a mirror-image triangle. As the paper says, either one will do.

understand.explanation: Euclid's recipe uses only two kinds of step: draw a circle, and join two points with a straight line. He draws a circle around A with radius AB, then a circle around B with radius BA. The point C where the circles cross lies on both of them, so it is one radius from A and one radius from B. Joining C to A and to B closes up a triangle on AB, with C as its third corner. Changing the length of AB only scales the picture. The guide to the paper adds that there are two choices for C, above or below AB, and either one will do. Here the crossing is simply drawn on a flat picture; later in the lesson we ask what justifies each step.
understand.quote: Describe the circle BCD with center A and radius AB. Again describe the circle ACE with center B and radius BA. Join the straight lines CA and CB from the point C at which the circles cut one another to the points A and B.

connect.caption: Euclid writes no equation. This is the model's rule for the construction, written as lengths. The blue r is the radius slider, which is also the length of AB (orange box). AC (green) and BC (red) are each one radius because C lies on both circles. Euclid states the same steps in words: circle BCD with centre A and radius AB, circle ACE with centre B and radius BA, then join CA and CB.

concepts.recap: Draw a circle of radius AB around each end of AB. Where the circles cross is C, one radius from both ends, and joining it to A and B builds the triangle, at any size and on either side.

concepts.title: The chain of reasons behind 'all sides equal'
concepts.idea: Each side is shown equal to AB for its own reason, and the rule 'things equal to the same thing are equal to one another' joins those facts into the conclusion that all three sides match.

terms.means: A general rule about equality that Euclid accepts without proof, such as 'things equal to the same thing are equal to one another' (C.N.1)
A short label beside a sentence of the proof, such as I.Def.15 or C.N.1, naming the rule that justifies that sentence

concepts.recap: AC = AB and BC = AB each come from the circle definition; C.N.1 joins them into AC = BC, and the triangle definition finishes the proof.

understand.explanation: From the last concept, point C lies on both circles, and Euclid now gives every claim its own reason. C lies on the circle centred at A, so AC equals AB by the definition of a circle (labelled I.Def.15). C also lies on the circle centred at B, so BC equals BA for the same reason. Those two facts do not yet compare AC with BC, so Euclid calls on a common notion, a general rule about equality accepted without proof: things equal to the same thing are equal to one another (C.N.1). That gives AC = BC, so all three sides match, and the definition of an equilateral triangle (I.Def.20) finishes the job. Each label such as I.Def.15 is a marginal reference: a note printed beside a sentence, added by editors rather than by Euclid, to show which rule backs that sentence.
understand.quote: And things which equal the same thing also equal one another, therefore AC also equals BC.

activities.prompt: Here is the proof's reasoning, one link at a time. For each link, notice which rule backs it. The rule's label is the marginal reference beside that sentence.

stages.label: Link 1: AC = AB
stages.text: Point C lies on the circle centred at A, with radius AB. Every point on a circle is one radius from the centre, so AC equals AB. Rule: the definition of a circle (I.Def.15).

stages.label: Link 2: BC = BA
stages.text: Point C also lies on the circle centred at B, with radius BA. By the same definition of a circle, BC equals BA. BA is the same segment as AB, named from the other end.

stages.label: Link 3: both equal AB
stages.text: Put the first two links together: AC equals AB, and BC equals AB. Both sides have been compared with the same thing, AB, but not yet with each other.

stages.label: Link 4: AC = BC
stages.text: Now the common notion does its work: things which equal the same thing also equal one another. AC and BC both equal AB, so AC equals BC. Rule: C.N.1.

stages.label: Link 5: the triangle is equilateral
stages.text: All three sides, AC, AB and BC, are equal. A triangle with three equal sides is equilateral by definition, so ABC is equilateral and stands on AB. Rule: I.Def.20. The proof ends with Q.E.F., 'which was to be done'.

activities.takeaway: No link is accepted just because it looks right in the picture. Each one points to a rule, and the common notion is the step that turns two separate comparisons with AB into one comparison between AC and BC.

activities.prompt: Put the links of the proof in the order they must come, so that each step uses only what has already been shown.
items: C is on the circle centred at A, so AC equals AB (I.Def.15)
C is on the circle centred at B, so BC equals BA (I.Def.15)
So each of AC and BC equals AB
Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another, so AC equals BC (C.N.1)
All three sides are equal, so triangle ABC is equilateral (I.Def.20)
activities.explanation: The two circle facts come first because everything else is built from them. Their order could be swapped, but both must be in place before you can say 'each equals AB'. C.N.1 can only be used once both sides have been compared with the same thing. The triangle definition comes last, because it needs all three sides already shown equal.
hints: Which steps use nothing except the circles themselves?
C.N.1 needs two things that both equal the same third thing. What has to be true before you can use it?
The definition of an equilateral triangle needs all three sides equal, so it can only be the final step.

activities.question: In the proof, which rule is what lets Euclid conclude that AC equals BC?

options.text: C.N.1: things which equal the same thing also equal one another
options.feedback: Yes. AC and BC have each been shown equal to AB, the same thing. C.N.1 is the general rule that joins those two facts into AC = BC.

options.text: I.Def.15: the definition of a circle
options.feedback: Not quite. The circle definition gives AC = AB and BC = BA, each from its own circle. No single circle has both A and B as its centre, so this definition alone never compares AC with BC directly.

options.text: I.Def.20: the definition of an equilateral triangle
options.feedback: This rule is used last, and in the other direction. It turns 'all three sides are equal' into 'the triangle is equilateral'. It cannot be used to prove that the sides are equal in the first place.

options.text: No rule is needed: you can see in the drawing that AC and BC are the same length
options.feedback: A drawing can suggest it, but a proof must give a reason for every claim. That is why the marginal reference C.N.1 sits beside this sentence, and here the rule is even quoted in full in the proof.

hints: AC and BC were each compared with one segment. Which one?
Look for the rule about things that equal the same thing.

activities.question: A made-up everyday case: a carpenter cuts one plank to exactly the length of a measuring stick. Later she cuts a second plank to exactly the length of the same stick. Without holding the planks side by side, what can she conclude, and why?

options.text: The two planks are the same length, because things equal to the same thing are equal to one another
options.feedback: Right. This is the same move as AC = BC. Each plank was compared with the stick, just as each side was compared with AB, and the common notion joins the two comparisons.

options.text: Nothing, until she lays the two planks side by side
options.feedback: Laying them side by side would confirm it, but the reasoning already settles it. C.N.1 lets you compare two things that were each matched to a third, without ever comparing them directly.

options.text: The planks match only if she cut them in the same order
options.feedback: The order of the cuts does not matter. In the proof, AC = AB and BC = BA could be shown in either order. All that matters is that both were matched to the same thing.

concepts.title: Who promised the circles cross?
concepts.idea: The proof needs the point C to exist, but no postulate of Euclid's guarantees that two circles meet; an extra rule such as 'if the radii add up to more than the distance between the centres, the circles meet' is needed.

predict.question: A later construction in the Elements (Proposition I.22, which the paper says needs the same rule) also draws two circles to find a crossing point. Here is a made-up case. Draw a line 10 long. Put a circle of radius 3 around one end and a circle of radius 4 around the other end. What happens?
options: The circles cross, and you get a triangle with sides 10, 3 and 4
The circles miss each other, so there is no crossing point and no triangle
The circles just touch at one point
You can't tell without drawing it very carefully
why: It is tempting to assume two circles always cross. Together they reach only 3 + 4 = 7, but the centres are 10 apart, so a gap of 3 is left.
Correct: the two radii add up to 7, which is less than the distance of 10 between the centres. The circles cannot reach each other, so there is no crossing point to build a triangle on.
Touching happens only when the two radii add up to exactly the distance between the centres. Here 7 falls short of 10, so they don't even touch.

A careful drawing would show the gap, but the comparison settles it without one. Compare the two radii added together with the distance between the centres. A drawing only shows one case; it can't prove anything.

terms.means: A starting rule Euclid accepts without proof, like 'a circle can be drawn around any centre'. It is his word for an axiom.
Two circles that touch at exactly one point without crossing
A step in a proof that is stated without enough reasons behind it

model.title: Two circles of the same size around A and B: pull the centres apart and watch C
model.note: Teaching model: A and B sit on a flat grid at −(r + extra)/2 and +(r + extra)/2, and both circles have the radius r. With the extra distance at 0 this is exactly Euclid's recipe, where AB equals the radius. Pulling the centres apart breaks the recipe on purpose, to show that crossing depends on a condition. Crossing points come from a coordinate formula, but Euclid used no coordinates or numbers. The model is the ordinary flat plane, where the extra rule happens to hold. The paper notes that other models of geometry exist where even Euclid's circles fail to meet. Numbers are illustrative, not from the paper.

steps.say: Same picture as before: a circle around A, a circle around B, and C where they cross. Right now this is exactly Euclid's recipe.
One new slider: it pushes B away from A. Both circles keep their size, and only the centres move apart. Watch C drop.
These boxes compare how far the two circles reach together with how far apart the centres are, and count the points on both circles.

explore.prompt: You've seen that crossing depends on how far the circles reach compared with how far apart the centres are. Now make the circles miss, then win the crossing back.

goals.text: Make the circles miss each other completely, so that no point lies on both of them.
hints: Which control moves the centres without changing the circles' size?
Watch the 'two radii minus the distance' box. What has to happen to it for a gap to open?
Each circle reaches one radius from its centre. The centres must end up farther apart than the two reaches added together, not just equal to them.

goals.text: Get the circles crossing at two points while the centres stay at least 5 units apart.
hints: Pushing the centres apart alone makes the circles miss. What else can you change?
Together the circles reach two radii. Compare that with the distance box: which one has to be bigger?
Grow the radius until two radii beat the distance. Then use the extra distance to keep the centres far enough apart. Remember that the radius also moves the centres a little.

feedback.correct: Right. The radii add up to 7 but the centres are 10 apart. The circles can't reach each other, so the crossing point the construction needs simply isn't there. Crossing is a condition you have to check, not something that comes free.
feedback.incorrect: It's natural to picture two circles overlapping, but crossing isn't automatic. Add the two radii and compare the total with the distance between the centres. Here 3 + 4 = 7 falls short of 10, so the circles miss and no crossing point exists.

steps.say: Start with Euclid's recipe. Each circle has radius AB, so the centres are one radius apart while the circles reach two radii together. They cross at two points.
Push the centres apart. The circles overlap less, and C sinks toward the line AB.

Now the centres are exactly two radii apart. The circles touch at one single point, which sits right on AB, and the triangle collapses flat. Circles that touch once without crossing are called tangent circles.
Push one step further and the circles miss. No point lies on both circles. There is no C, so there is nothing to build a triangle on.
Walk P around circle A. Its distance to B never shrinks to one radius, so P never lands on circle B.
So the circles cross only when the two radii added together are more than the distance between the centres. Crossing is a condition, not a fact about all circles.
Back to Euclid's recipe: AB plus AB is more than AB, so here the circles do cross. But none of Euclid's postulates, his starting rules, says that circles meeting this condition must cross.
So when the proof says 'the point C at which the circles cut one another', it leans on something it never stated. That is a logical gap. The picture shows C, but a picture is not a reason.

understand.explanation: Euclid's proof talks about 'the point C at which the circles cut one another' as if that point simply had to be there. As the model shows, two circles cross only when their radii added together are more than the distance between their centres: at exactly equal they just touch, and beyond that they miss. In Euclid's recipe the condition holds, because AB plus AB is more than AB, but none of his postulates says that such circles must actually meet. The paper points out that the only postulate promising a point exists is the parallel postulate, which has nothing to do with circles. It argues that an extra rule is needed, such as 'if the sum of the radii is greater than the distance between the centres, the circles intersect'. It also notes that there are models of geometry in which these circles do not meet at all, so a drawing on flat paper can't settle the question.
understand.quote: Near the beginning of the proof, the point C is mentioned where the circles are supposed to intersect, but there is no justification for its existence. The only one of Euclid’s postulate that says a point exists the parallel postulate, and that postulate is not relevant here.
understand.quote_where: Guide, 'Critiques of the proof: Why does the point C exist?'

check.task: Put the model in a state where the circles touch at exactly one point. In a drawing with thick lines this case could easily pass for crossing or for missing.
check.hint: Touching sits right on the border between crossing and missing: the two radii added together exactly equal the distance between the centres.
check.misconception: If a drawing shows the circles meeting, that proves they meet. In fact a drawing can't tell touching from crossing or from missing by a hair, and it shows only one case. Only a stated rule can promise the point exists.

connect.caption: The paper states this rule in words; here it is written with the model's symbols, not Euclid's. Both radii are the slider r, AB is the distance box, and the crossing count shows whether C exists. In Euclid's recipe r equals AB, so AB + AB beats AB and the rule promises C. Nothing in Euclid's own list does. For circles of different sizes, a careful version must also rule out one circle sitting inside the other. Equal radii avoid that.

concepts.recap: Euclid's circles do cross, but none of his postulates promises it. The proof needs an extra rule: circles whose radii add up to more than the distance between their centres must meet.

concepts.title: More hidden assumptions: flat figures and merging sides
concepts.idea: Besides the missing point C, the proof never shows the sides lie in one plane, and it never rules out sides AC and BC merging before they reach C (Zeno's objection), which needs the rule that two straight lines meet in at most one point.

terms.means: A flat shape that lies entirely on one flat surface, like a drawing on a sheet of paper
A stretch that two lines share, where they run together as one, like two roads merging into a single lane
A case where every stated step still holds but the conclusion fails, which shows the argument has a gap

concepts.recap: Euclid's most obvious proof relies on facts his rules never state: that the circles cross, and that two straight lines cannot share a stretch.

understand.explanation: You have already seen one gap: none of Euclid's rules promises that the two circles cross at C. The commentator who wrote this guide to the Elements names two more. First, a triangle is a plane figure, a flat shape lying wholly on one flat surface, but the proof never shows that the three sides lie on one flat surface. The results that would show this, XI.1 and XI.2, come much later, in the part of the book about solid (three-dimensional) geometry. Second, Zeno of Sidon pointed out that AC and BC might meet at a point E before C and then run together along a common segment EC. The region they enclose would then be triangle ABE, which is isosceles rather than equilateral, so it is a counterexample. Ruling it out needs a rule Euclid never states: two straight lines can meet in at most one point.
understand.quote: What needs to be shown (or assumed as a postulate) is that two infinitely extended straight lines can meet in at most one point.
understand.quote_where: Guide, 'Critiques of the proof': Why does ABC contain an equilateral triangle?

activities.prompt: Compare the figure Euclid intends with the figures his steps fail to rule out. In every case AC still equals AB and BC still equals BA, so each step of the proof is still true.

cases.label: Euclid's intended figure
cases.text: Line AC and line BC set off from A and from B and touch only at C. Together with AB they close off one triangle, ABC, and its three sides are equal. This is the figure the proof assumes.

cases.label: Zeno's merged sides
cases.text: AC and BC meet early, at a point E, and then run together along a shared stretch EC up to C. The region they close off is ABE, not ABC. AE and BE are equal to each other but shorter than AB, so ABE is isosceles (two equal sides), not equilateral.

cases.label: The 'necklace of bubbles'
cases.text: The commentator goes further than Zeno. The two sides could meet and separate many times on the way to C, so the region they enclose looks like a string of bubbles rather than one triangle. Nothing in Euclid's stated rules forbids this.

activities.takeaway: The proof shows that three lengths are equal. It never shows that those lengths form one triangle. To close the gap, you need the rule that two straight lines can meet in at most one point. Then AC and BC cannot touch before C, and they cannot share a stretch.

activities.title: Justified step or hidden gap?
activities.prompt: Sort each claim the proof makes or needs. Put it under 'Justified' if one of Euclid's stated definitions, postulates or common notions supports it. Put it under 'Gap' if the proof uses it without any stated reason.

cards.text: AC equals AB, because A is the centre of the circle through B and C.
cards.feedback: Justified. The definition of a circle (I.Def.15) says every point on it is the same distance from the centre.

cards.text: BC equals BA, because B is the centre of the other circle.
cards.feedback: Justified by the same definition of a circle, I.Def.15, applied to the circle centred at B.

cards.text: AC equals BC, because both equal AB.
cards.feedback: Justified. This is Common Notion 1: things which equal the same thing also equal one another.

cards.text: A triangle with three equal sides is called equilateral.
cards.feedback: Justified. This is simply the definition of 'equilateral' (I.Def.20). The trouble is not this definition. It is whether the sides really form a single triangle.

cards.text: The two circles cross at a point C.
cards.feedback: Gap. The commentator notes that no postulate of Euclid's makes the point C exist. This was the previous concept's gap.

cards.text: The three sides lie together on one flat surface.
cards.feedback: Gap. A triangle must be a plane figure, but this is never shown here. XI.1 and XI.2 claim it, and the commentator says they logically should come before I.1. They sit in Book XI, though, with solid geometry. The commentator also calls the reasoning in XI.1 faulty.

cards.text: Lines AC and BC first meet at C and do not share any stretch before it.
cards.feedback: Gap. This is Zeno's objection. The fix is the rule that two straight lines meet in at most one point, and Euclid never proves or assumes it.

activities.takeaway: Every equality in the proof has a stated reason. What has no stated reason is the picture behind the equalities: that C exists, that the figure is flat, and that the sides form one triangle.

activities.prompt: Follow the ancient dispute over Zeno's objection, as reported by Proclus and judged by the commentator.

stages.label: 1. The objector
stages.text: Zeno of Sidon was an Epicurean philosopher of the early first century B.C.E. He is a different person from Zeno of Elea, who was famous for paradoxes and lived long before Euclid. Zeno of Sidon objected that the proof never shows the sides do not meet before they reach the corners.

stages.label: 2. The counterexample
stages.text: Suppose AC and BC meet at E before C and then share the stretch EC. The figure they close off is ABE, which is isosceles, not equilateral. Every step of Euclid's proof still holds, but the conclusion fails.

stages.label: 3. What Zeno saw was needed
stages.text: Zeno recognised that defeating his counterexample needs a new assumption: straight lines cannot have a common segment.

stages.label: 4. The reply
stages.text: According to Proclus, Posidonius wrote a book refuting Zeno. Proclus also relates a supposed proof that straight lines cannot share a segment, the same argument later found in Proposition XI.1.

stages.label: 5. The commentator's verdict
stages.text: The commentator judges that Zeno's critique is sound and the refutation is faulty. Proclus and Posidonius relied on properties of lines and circles that were never proven and never openly assumed as postulates.

stages.label: 6. The wider gap
stages.text: The commentator adds that far more cases remain open than Zeno's single example, such as the 'necklace of bubbles'. The needed rule must be either proved or simply assumed: two infinitely extended straight lines can meet in at most one point.

activities.takeaway: An argument that looks airtight can rest on facts nobody wrote down. Here even the attempted repair used unstated facts, so the honest fix is to add the rule as a postulate.

activities.question: In the dispute over Zeno's objection, which side does the commentator back?

options.text: Zeno: his critique is sound, and Posidonius's refutation is faulty.
options.feedback: Correct. The guide says plainly that the critique is sound and the refutation faulty, because the reply relied on properties that were never proven and never assumed.

options.text: Posidonius: his book settled the question in Euclid's favour.
options.feedback: Not supported. Proclus says Posidonius refuted Zeno, but the commentator disagrees and calls that refutation faulty.

options.text: Neither: the objection is a muddled version of Zeno of Elea's paradoxes.
options.feedback: This is a misattribution. The guide specifically warns not to confuse Zeno of Sidon with Zeno of Elea. It treats the objection as a real logical gap.

options.text: Both: Zeno found a real gap, and Proclus's proof (later XI.1) closed it.
options.feedback: Half right. Zeno did find a real gap, but the commentator says the proof Proclus relates is faulty, so it does not close the gap.

hints: Look again at stage 5 of the dispute.
The commentator uses the words 'sound' and 'faulty'. Which side gets which word?

activities.question: Step back to the whole proof. Which of these facts does Euclid's first proof rely on even though none of his postulates or common notions states it? Select all that apply.

options.text: The two circles actually cross, so the point C exists.
options.feedback: Yes. No postulate of Euclid's makes C exist. A rule such as 'if the radii add up to more than the distance between the centres, the circles meet' is needed.

options.text: Two straight lines cannot run together and share a stretch. They meet in at most one point.
options.feedback: Yes. Without this rule, Zeno's merged-sides figure and the 'necklace of bubbles' are not ruled out.

options.text: Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another.
options.feedback: No. This one is stated: it is Common Notion 1, and the proof cites it by name.

options.text: Every point on a circle is the same distance from its centre.
options.feedback: No. This is stated in the definition of a circle (I.Def.15). It is what makes AC equal AB and BC equal BA.

hints: Two options are cited in the proof's margin notes. Two are not.
Recall the earlier gap about C, and the gap Zeno raised.
